Hale-Bopp. One of the brightest and most spectacularly active comets of the modern era, discovered independently in 1995 and reaching perihelion on April 1st, 1997. Its passage was visible to the naked eye for over a year, making it a signature astronomical event of the 1990s and sparking global public interest.

The comet was discovered independently by Thomas Bopp, an amateur, and Alan Hale, a professional, on July 23rd, 1995. Per convention, it was named for both discoverers. Hale-Bopp is an extremely active comet. It developed two distinct tails — one of dust and one of ionized gas — and brightened far more than models predicted, outgassing copiously as it approached the Sun.

Visibility to the naked eye extended from mid-1996 through mid-1997, an unusually long window that made it a cultural phenomenon and inspired public observatory events worldwide. Its orbital period is roughly 2,533 years. Its last perihelion was around 4,385 BCE, placing previous visibility during early Egyptian civilization.

The nucleus is estimated at 40 kilometers across, one of the largest comets on record. This immense size powered the exceptional outgassing and brightness. The ion tail, which follows the solar wind, reached more than 40 million kilometers in length, while the dust tail curved behind its orbital motion. As a canonical example of a bright, long-period comet, Hale-Bopp remains the archetype for public interest in cometary astronomy. It was likely an Oort Cloud immigrant, ejected inward by stellar perturbations, an explanation for its multi-millennia periodicity.
